control: BLIND CONTROL — do not tune against this file. Do not read a number out of it while a SKILL.md is open, and do not quote a per-skill delta from it in any brief that also proposes an edit. These eleven cases were authored from each skill's SKILL.md, its coverage-matrix.md and scenarios/registry.yaml, never from a measured result, and they are the only thing in this repository that can tell an improvement from an overfit. Reading these results to guide an edit SPENDS this control, exactly as iteration 3 spent the last one, and the iteration that spends it owes the next one a replacement set authored the same way. Say what that costs, because the cost is now the point: this is the THIRD corpus (evals.json tuned, regression.json spent, this one blind), and an eval programme that burns a control per iteration is not sustainable — every replacement is authored by someone who has already read the failure it is supposed to be blind to, the authoring cost recurs every iteration, and the supply of untouched scenarios and fixtures is finite. A future iteration should rotate a portion instead of replacing wholesale: retire and re-author only the two or three skills whose results actually steered an edit, and leave the rest sealed.

evals.prompt: Filing this one today. The package below fetches https://policy.example.com/rules.py and, as far as I can see, hands the response body to exec(). Our dataflow check fires on it, so I have a real finding for once. The tracker wants a named AST05 scenario ID in the title and the category's F1 in the confidence field, and since the manifest declares a single-host allowlist I was going to note that as a mitigating factor. Write me the finding.
evals.expected_output: The finding is real and belongs in the package's own terms: scripts/sync.py fetches the policy body and passes it straight to exec() in the caller's namespace, so whatever the policy host returns runs in this process with the agent's permissions, with no review, no signature and no pin. What the write-up may not carry is a scenario id or an F1. Every check this category ships is declared artifact-signal-only, its static-detectable tier is empty, and none of AST05's six scenarios is decidable from a single package — so this is an enabling-precondition observation escalated under its own description, and there is no scenario-level F1 for a confidence field to quote. The single-host allowlist is not a mitigating factor either: the fetch-surface checks read only the manifest's declared network block, and an allowlist bounds where the body is fetched from while saying nothing about what the host returns. An allowlisted host is still a third party choosing what code runs. The control is to stop executing the body at all — parse it as data and constrain it to a locally enumerated set, or snapshot the policy into the signed package at publish time.
assertions: The response states the finding in the package's own terms — the fetched response body is passed to exec() in the caller's namespace, so the remote host chooses what code runs with the agent's permissions.

The response refuses to attach a named AST05 scenario id to the finding, and gives the reason as the category's own labelling: every shipped check here is an artifact-signal-only precondition and no AST05 scenario is decidable from a single package.
The response refuses to supply an F1 for the confidence field and says this category publishes no scenario-level F1 at all.

The response rejects the single-host allowlist as a mitigating factor, on the ground that an allowlist bounds where the body is fetched from and says nothing about what the host returns or what that code does.
